newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Political row deepens over Taiwan law and order.
newsitem.headline: Political row deepens over Taiwan law and order.

text.p: A row over Taiwan's shaky law and order intensified on Tuesday as President Lee Teng-hui's party shot down a parliamentary challenge minutes after opposition lawmakers thwarted Lee's annual National Assembly address.
The political crisis, which has shaken Lee's government as well as Taiwan's jittery financial markets, showed no signs of abating.

Vice-president and Premier Lien Chan, under intense pressure to resign, was expected to unveil a modest cabinet reshuffle on Wednesday, but opposition lawmakers -- and a broad swathe of the public -- say anything short of Lien's sacking is not enough.
"The intensifying political confrontation between the ruling and opposition parties will have a significant impact on Taiwan," said National Taiwan University commentator Lu Ya-li.

"With both ruling and opposition parties showing no signs of concession, the stalemate will slow the pace of many crucial political and constitutional reforms. The Nationalists should adopt a large-scale cabinet reshuffle to solve the crisis."

Lien late on Monday appeared ready to heed demands for his head, telling a television call-in show that he was willing to resign -- but not before crucial constitutional reforms are enacted by the National Assembly in July.

"The recent situation has caused people unease. It's time for me to consider taking responsibility," he said. "But many limits and circumstances prevent me from leaving my current post. That is why I decide to stay on."

The day started badly for Lee, who was elected in March last year with a landslide but whose popularity has slipped over his government's failure to solve a spate of horrific crimes. The most recent was the kidnap, torture and murder of a teenage girl.

Opposition politicians, incensed over Lee's crime-fighting record, donned robes bearing protest slogans and filibustered the largely ceremonial National Assembly, effectively preventing Lee from delivering a keynote annual address.

The president, whose speech had already been made public in draft form, left the assembly hall without commenting on calls for him to apologise for what he recently described as "worsening social law and order".

The assembly was due to reconvene on Wednesday, but it was not known when, or if, Lee would return to deliver his speech. In it he blamed the crime rate in part on the ignorance of people about their responsibilities in Taiwan's fledgling democracy.
Lee's forces fared somewhat better across town at the Legislative Yuan, Taiwan's rambunctious parliament.

Just minutes after Lee's National Assembly snub, lawmakers from his ruling Nationalist Party pulled out all the stops to vote down a motion urging Lee to sack Premier Lien and order a sweeping cabinet reshuffle.
Analysts said passage of the non-binding resolution could have deepened public anxieties and rattled Taiwan's financial markets, which have reeled through the crisis.

As political uncertainty deepened, the stock market slipped 0.18 percent. On Monday it plunged 3.72 percent, its biggest single-day loss since January 1996. The Taiwan dollar has also fallen sharply in the last two days.
Lien has given no signs of giving up the vice-presidency to which he was elected in 1996. He serves simultaneously as premier, or cabinet chief, at the president's discretion.

Anti-government sentiment erupted on April 28 when police found the 17-year-old daughter of a prominent actress floating dead in a river. A massive manhunt, complete with late-night checkpoints by heavily armed police, has failed to catch three key suspects for Pai Hsiao-yen's kidnap and murder.
The crime rekindled anger over the unsolved gangland-style murder of a county magistrate and seven others in his home in November and an opposition leader's murder two weeks later.
More than 50,000 people demonstrated in Taipei on May 4 to demand the resignation of Lien and a cabinet reshuffle and plan a similar march on Sunday.
